label: paragraph_title

label: paragraph_title
text: WHITE—THOMPSON

label: text
text: There was a large attendance of friends of Mr. Nowell Bernard White and Miss Pearl "Chifford Thompson" on the occasion of their marriage on Saturday afternoon at St. John's Cathedral, also later at the Hongkong Hotel roof garden. Mr. White is the son of the late Mr. H. J. B. White and Mrs. Rose White and the manager of Mac's Cafeteria at the Hongkong Hotel. Miss Thompson is the daughter of the late Mr. Richard Thompson and of Mrs. S. Thompson, Philadelphia, and arrived in the Colony by the s.s. Empress of Australia.

label: text
text: The bride, who looked charming in a dress of georgette and face with bridal veil; carried a lovely bouquet of carnations. She was given away by Mr. J. P. Bourne. Her attendants were Miss Rose White (sister of the bridegroom) and Miss Stella Bander, both of whom wore

label: text
text: Mrs. M. A. R. Souza was marron of honour.

label: text
text: Mr. G. H. White, brother of the bridegroom, was Best Man.

label: text
text: The ceremony was performed by the Rev. T. B. Powell.

label: text
text: At the reception the healths of the young couple' and of their parents was proposed by Mrs. J. H. Tuggart. The roof garden looked prodigy than over with floral decorations and a huge wedding bell of flowers and foliage suspended from the ceiling.

label: paragraph_title
text: CORRESPONDENCE

label: paragraph_title
text: Drenching Street Passengers.

label: text
text: (To the Editor of the China Mail).

label: text
text: Sir,—It is from personal and eye-witness experience that when any one passes along a Chinese street he is often subject to receiving a downpour of dirty water, some kind of dirt or spittle, etc.

label: text
text: But now I regret to state that this happens not only in the Chinese streets but also among European quarters. I have seen a man drenched to the very skin while he was passing along the Praya East at the building adjacent to the Royal Canteen and at the same spot at another time another man also was supplied with a plate of something like macaroni soup. There are many more cases, which, when put down, will fill many columns.

label: text
text: Personally I was once drenched at the Post Office Tram station and another time at the Butterfield & Swire Building. For all these instances the culprits seemed to get off scotfree, because if the sufferer were to go into the house or building to inquire he would certainly receive a hot answer or might even be charged with trespassing. For the welfare of the public I would like to call the attention of the government to inflict a severe punishment to those uncivilized culprits when caught.

label: text
text: Again I wish to point out that Hongkong is scarcely anything more than a granite mountain. Consequently, houses are generally built on terraces. Therefore masters and mistresses of those concerned should take more care of their servants and not to allow them to throw down any rubbish to a lower terrace, for that will not only give extra trouble to the servants, but also make the place very unsightly. At the present time many roofs are decorated with mango fruit stones, etc. If the fear of punishment by the Government or the horror of being trented alike does not force them to take more care of their servants, let common sense and humanity induce them to do so.

label: text
text: In conclusion. I'have the honour to thank the Editor for thus encroaching so much space in his valuable paper.
